context.concept_name: Execute Python AWS automation in an isolated dependency environment after active registry language preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Execute Python AWS automation in an isolated environment

required_facts.statement: A virtual environment isolates the Python interpreter context and installed packages used by an application.
Create one with python -m venv ENV_DIR and activate it using the platform’s activation command, such as source ENV_DIR/bin/activate on Unix.
Install supplied dependencies with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt inside the environment, inspect them with python -m pip list, and run the supplied script with that interpreter.
Confirm the approved AWS profile and Region through the supplied credential configuration before running AWS automation.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Python automation script has a requirements file. Before running it against AWS, prepare an isolated dependency environment and confirm the intended operator context.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A virtual environment isolates the Python interpreter context and installed packages used by an application.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create one with python -m venv ENV_DIR and activate it using the platform’s activation command, such as source ENV_DIR/bin/activate on Unix.

Install supplied dependencies with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt inside the environment, inspect them with python -m pip list, and run the supplied script with that interpreter.

Confirm the approved AWS profile and Region through the supplied credential configuration before running AWS automation.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use python -m venv ENV_DIR with the supplied directory name, then activate it with the command for your platform; source ENV_DIR/bin/activate is the Unix example. Inside that environment, install requirements.txt with the stated pip command and inspect the package list. Run the supplied script with that environment's interpreter only after confirming the approved AWS profile and Region through its credential configuration. Record the environment and context used alongside the script outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Dependency isolation and AWS target selection are separate checks. A virtual environment isolates interpreter context and installed packages; it does not replace confirming the approved AWS profile and Region.

video_need.reason: A short environment and dependency setup demonstration helps locate the active interpreter, but the supplied command sequence suffices in text.

practice_anchor.objective: Create and activate one virtual environment, install and inspect the supplied dependencies, confirm the approved AWS profile and Region, and run the supplied automation script with that environment's interpreter.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied script runs with the activated environment's interpreter after dependency inspection and AWS context confirmation, without installing packages into the host's global Python environment.

live_code.required_skill: Execute the supplied Python automation using an isolated interpreter and dependency context.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide the supplied automation script, requirements.txt, an environment directory name, the platform's activation command, and supplied credential configuration identifying the approved AWS profile and Region. Begin with no project virtual environment active; script editing is not required.
live_code.observable_success: One virtual environment is created and activated; dependencies are installed and listed through its interpreter; the supplied credential configuration is checked against the approved profile and Region before execution; the supplied script outcome and environment/context used are recorded. Global Python packages remain unchanged.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the active virtual environment, environment-scoped dependency installation and package list, and separate approved AWS profile and Region confirmation visible before the supplied script executes.

teaching_notes: Require external Python and shell preparation; activation paths are platform-specific templates.

context.concept_name: Extract structured AWS CLI inventory across paginated results

coverage.learning_objective: Extract AWS CLI inventory across pagination

required_facts.statement: The AWS CLI automatically follows service-side pagination for supported commands unless automatic pagination is disabled.
Use an explicit --profile and --region with --output json for structured inventory and avoid --no-paginate when the full listing is required.

--page-size changes service-call page size rather than the total output count; --max-items limits output and a returned NextToken must be resumed with --starting-token when manually collecting the remainder.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An inventory task needs all results in one approved account and Region. Page controls affect how results are retrieved or bounded, so read them before claiming that a listing is complete.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The AWS CLI automatically follows service-side pagination for supported commands unless automatic pagination is disabled.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use an explicit --profile and --region with --output json for structured inventory and avoid --no-paginate when the full listing is required.

--page-size changes service-call page size rather than the total output count; --max-items limits output and a returned NextToken must be resumed with --starting-token when manually collecting the remainder.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied supported inventory command with explicit profile and Region and JSON output. For the full listing, keep automatic pagination enabled rather than adding --no-paginate. If the exercise deliberately uses --max-items to collect a bounded portion, retain the returned NextToken and resume with --starting-token for the remainder. Changing --page-size adjusts service-call page size; it is not the same as limiting total output with --max-items. Keep the continuation evidence with the inventory.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A smaller page size does not mean a smaller total inventory. Distinguish service-call page size from the output limit, and do not discard a continuation token when manually collecting the remainder.

video_need.reason: A brief page-size/output-limit comparison helps interpret continuation tokens; the bounded pagination rules are fully stated in text.

media.group_title: How automatic pagination builds a complete inventory

segments.label: How the AWS CLI collects a full listing across service pages
segments.summary: A supported listing operation can require several service requests rather than one. Using an EC2 snapshot listing as the example, the speaker explains that each response indicates whether more results remain. The AWS CLI automatically requests subsequent pages until the service reports no more results, then assembles the complete list in memory and returns it as command output.

bridge_note.before: Watch how service responses tell the AWS CLI whether another page is needed, and how automatic pagination assembles those pages into one listing.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains automatic collection, but not disabling it, explicit profile/Region/JSON settings, or page-size, output-limit, and token-resumption controls. The text covers those requirements for a complete, consistently scoped inventory.

practice_anchor.objective: Export one sandbox resource inventory using a supplied supported AWS CLI inventory command with explicit --profile, --region, and --output json. Keep automatic pagination enabled for the full listing, then use a bounded exercise to practise retaining a returned NextToken and resuming with --starting-token.
practice_anchor.success: The full-listing export uses the supplied sandbox profile and Region consistently and does not use --no-paginate or an output limit. In the bounded exercise, the learner preserves each returned NextToken, resumes in the same context until no continuation remains, and distinguishes --page-size from --max-items.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make successive service requests and responses visible, showing automatic collection until no results remain alongside a bounded --max-items result whose NextToken is passed to --starting-token. Keep the same explicit profile and Region visible throughout, and distinguish service-call page size from total output count.

teaching_notes: Apply pagination only to supported commands; do not invent an inventory command or API continuation format.

context.concept_name: Hand over an actionable operational runbook

required_facts.statement: A runbook documents procedures for a known operational outcome and should be usable by the operator performing the task.
Write the task’s preconditions, ordered actions and expected results so execution can be checked rather than inferred.
Include failure-handling and escalation instructions identifying when routine execution must stop and who takes over.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Another operator must perform a known task without relying on your memory. A useful runbook makes the conditions for acting and the evidence for advancing explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A runbook documents procedures for a known operational outcome and should be usable by the operator performing the task.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Write the task’s preconditions, ordered actions and expected results so execution can be checked rather than inferred.

Include failure-handling and escalation instructions identifying when routine execution must stop and who takes over.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For a supplied restart task, write its preconditions, approved ordered actions and expected results from the established procedure. Include the condition that stops routine work and name the escalation recipient. Read the draft as the receiving operator: can each expected result be checked before advancing? Replace an instruction such as confirm it worked with the supplied observable result. Do not invent a recovery action outside the approved procedure.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A list of actions alone is not an actionable runbook. Preconditions, expected results and failure/escalation instructions are needed so the operator can check execution rather than infer success.

video_need.reason: The handoff is a short document structure and expected-result check; a sample runbook table suffices.

practice_anchor.objective: Produce one bounded runbook for a supplied restart task using its established procedure and owner information. Document the outcome, preconditions, ordered actions, checkable expected results, failure-handling instructions, stop condition and escalation recipient.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted runbook lets another operator identify when the task may begin, which approved actions occur in order, how to check each expected result, when routine execution must stop and who takes over. It introduces no actions outside the supplied procedure.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make a sample restart runbook visible with its outcome and preconditions, followed by ordered action rows showing expected results, failure-handling instructions, stop conditions and escalation recipients.

teaching_notes: Use established procedures and owners; defer live incident execution to the later runbook-recovery concept.

context.concept_name: Operate an EKS Pod using supplied cluster-access setup

coverage.learning_objective: Inspect and operate an EKS Pod

required_facts.statement: A Pod groups containers with shared networking and storage and has a lifecycle distinct from the controller that may replace it.
Pod phases include Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown; phase alone is not a complete diagnosis of container health.
Use kubectl get pod NAME, kubectl describe pod NAME and kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER to inspect status, scheduling or runtime events and container output.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EKS workload has a Pod that appears to be running. The operator still needs evidence about its containers and events. Pod phase is one lifecycle observation, not a complete health diagnosis.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Pod groups containers with shared networking and storage and has a lifecycle distinct from the controller that may replace it.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Pod phases include Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown; phase alone is not a complete diagnosis of container health.

Use kubectl get pod NAME, kubectl describe pod NAME and kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER to inspect status, scheduling or runtime events and container output.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Using the supplied cluster access setup, substitute the approved Pod name into kubectl get pod NAME. Record its phase, then inspect kubectl describe pod NAME for scheduling or runtime events. Use kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER for the intended container's output. Suppose the phase reads Running while the supplied events and logs show a container problem. Preserve those observations together rather than deciding that Running settles health. A Pod groups containers with shared networking and storage; its lifecycle is distinct from a controller that may replace it. This exercise inspects the Pod and its container output, not the controller's desired-replica reconciliation or cluster administration.

If the Pod is Pending, use its described scheduling events as evidence rather than applying a correction inferred from the phase label alone. If it is Running, inspect the intended container's runtime events and output. The same inspection sequence accommodates different phases because it records what happened at the Pod and container boundaries. An unrelated container's output is not evidence about the one named in the exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Running is a Pod phase, not a complete diagnosis of container health. Other phases include Pending, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown, but the phase list does not replace inspection of events and the intended container's logs.

video_need.reason: Pod phase, runtime events and container logs are separate changing observations that benefit from a live inspection demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Inspect one seeded failing Pod using the supplied cluster access and image. Substitute the supplied Pod and container names into kubectl get pod NAME, kubectl describe pod NAME and kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER, then identify the failure supported by the observations.
practice_anchor.success: Record the Pod phase, relevant scheduling or runtime events, and the intended container's output. Identify the seeded failure using those observations together, without treating Running as proof of container health or changing the workload.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied Pod's status, described events and intended container's logs together, making the distinction between Pod phase and container failure evidence visible.

teaching_notes: Use supplied cluster access; leave Deployment reconciliation and self-managed cluster administration out of scope.

context.concept_name: Operate an RDS managed database as the native backup-resource foundation

required_facts.statement: An RDS DB instance has an identifier, engine, endpoint and operational status that can be inspected in the console or through describe-db-instances.
Inspect the intended DB instance and verify its engine and status before attempting the supplied database connection.
Connect using the supplied endpoint, database client and approved credentials, then run the supplied query to check the data marker; instance status alone does not verify application data.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A managed database is available for an approved connection test. Verify the intended instance and the data marker separately; a resource status does not answer whether the expected application data is present.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An RDS DB instance has an identifier, engine, endpoint and operational status that can be inspected in the console or through describe-db-instances.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the intended DB instance and verify its engine and status before attempting the supplied database connection.

Connect using the supplied endpoint, database client and approved credentials, then run the supplied query to check the data marker; instance status alone does not verify application data.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Locate the supplied DB instance identifier in the console or describe-db-instances result. Compare its engine and operational status with the exercise requirements before using the supplied endpoint, client and approved credentials. Run the supplied query and retain its data-marker result. If the status is acceptable but the query does not return the expected marker, report that distinction rather than calling the data check successful. Record the instance identity and endpoint with the safe query outcome so the test can be tied to the intended database. This is bounded database operation with a supplied query, not a lesson in authoring SQL or selecting database capacity.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An acceptable instance status does not verify application data. The instance inspection checks identity, engine and status; the supplied connection and query check the data marker. Neither result should be used as a substitute for the other.

video_need.reason: A brief instance-to-endpoint walkthrough helps tie the safe query to the intended database; text covers the supplied check.

practice_anchor.objective: Inspect the supplied sandbox RDS instance using preconfigured networking. Verify its identifier, engine and operational status before connecting with the supplied endpoint, database client and approved credentials, then run the supplied query to check the expected data marker.
practice_anchor.success: The recorded identifier matches the intended instance, its engine and status are compared with the supplied requirements, and its endpoint is recorded. The supplied query result is compared with the expected data marker, with the data-check outcome reported separately from instance status.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the intended RDS instance's identifier, engine, operational status and endpoint visible alongside the supplied query result and expected data marker, distinguishing resource inspection from application-data verification without exposing credentials.

teaching_notes: Use supplied client and query; do not teach SQL syntax or database capacity selection.

context.concept_name: Protect recoverable S3 objects with versioning and lifecycle controls

coverage.learning_objective: Protect S3 data recovery with versioning

required_facts.statement: S3 versioning retains multiple versions of an object, including versions displaced by overwrites.
In a versioning-enabled bucket, a simple delete ordinarily creates a delete marker rather than removing prior versions; deleting a specified version permanently removes it.
To restore an overwritten object, copy the selected prior version to the same key to create a new current version; to undo a simple deletion, remove its delete marker to expose the preceding version.
Inspect noncurrent-version expiration and other lifecycle rules so required recoverable versions remain for the required window.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An S3 object was overwritten or simply deleted, and the lab requires an earlier version to remain recoverable. Versioning, restoration method and lifecycle expiry all affect the available recovery path.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: S3 versioning retains multiple versions of an object, including versions displaced by overwrites.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
In a versioning-enabled bucket, a simple delete ordinarily creates a delete marker rather than removing prior versions; deleting a specified version permanently removes it.

To restore an overwritten object, copy the selected prior version to the same key to create a new current version; to undo a simple deletion, remove its delete marker to expose the preceding version.

Inspect noncurrent-version expiration and other lifecycle rules so required recoverable versions remain for the required window.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the approved bucket contains two versions of releases/orders.zip and the newer one overwrote the earlier content. Select the required prior version and copy it to the same key; that creates a new current version with the selected content. For a separate simple-deletion case, inspect the delete marker and remove that marker to expose the preceding version. These are different recovery operations, so identify the actual case before acting. Inspect noncurrent-version expiration and other supplied lifecycle rules against the required recovery window. A retained prior version is useful only while it remains available under those controls. Do not delete a specified needed version: that operation permanently removes that version.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A simple delete in a versioning-enabled bucket ordinarily creates a delete marker; it is not equivalent to permanently deleting a specified version. Keep ordinarily in the explanation, and check lifecycle rules rather than assuming versioning alone preserves every version indefinitely.

video_need.reason: Version lists, delete markers and recovery actions benefit from a controlled before-and-after object restoration demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Enable versioning on the approved sandbox bucket and apply the supplied recovery-preserving lifecycle policy for releases/orders.zip.
practice_anchor.success: The bucket reports versioning as enabled, the supplied lifecycle policy is applied, and inspection of noncurrent-version expiration and other applicable rules confirms that required versions remain recoverable for the supplied recovery window.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the approved bucket's enabled versioning and applicable lifecycle rules alongside the version history for releases/orders.zip. Make distinct recovery results visible: copying an approved prior version creates a new current version, while removing a delete marker exposes the preceding version.

teaching_notes: Use approved versions and recovery window; distinguish marker removal from copying a prior version.

context.concept_name: Publish a container image to ECR after external Docker preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Publish a container image to ECR

required_facts.statement: ECR stores container images in repositories and assigns image digests that identify image content.
Authenticate Docker with aws ecr get-login-password --region REGION piped to docker login --username AWS --password-stdin REGISTRY.
Tag the already-built image with REGISTRY/REPOSITORY:TAG and run docker push with that reference.
Use docker pull REGISTRY/REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST to retrieve the exact image and verify publisher and consumer access with their approved identities.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An already-built container image must reach an approved repository and then be retrieved as the exact published content. Keep the publication reference and the content digest separate in the evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: ECR stores container images in repositories and assigns image digests that identify image content.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Authenticate Docker with aws ecr get-login-password --region REGION piped to docker login --username AWS --password-stdin REGISTRY.

Tag the already-built image with REGISTRY/REPOSITORY:TAG and run docker push with that reference.

Use docker pull REGISTRY/REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST to retrieve the exact image and verify publisher and consumer access with their approved identities.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Substitute the supplied Region and registry in the authentication pipeline from get-login-password to docker login. Tag the already-built image with the approved REGISTRY/REPOSITORY:TAG and push that reference. Record the published image digest, then use the supplied digest in docker pull REGISTRY/REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST for the consumer test. Verify publisher and consumer access with their respective approved identities rather than using one identity for both roles. The digest identifies image content, while the repository and tag provide the publication reference in this exercise. The task begins with a built image and does not ask for Dockerfile authoring or a new container build process.

Write the publication and consumption references side by side: the push uses REGISTRY/REPOSITORY:TAG, and the exact-content pull uses REGISTRY/REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST. Verify that the digest is the one recorded after publishing. Testing publisher push permission does not establish consumer pull permission, so preserve both identity-specific outcomes. This separates content identity from the two access roles without rebuilding the supplied image.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Publication is not the same as verified consumption. Push with the approved publisher, then retrieve the exact digest under the approved consumer and check its access. Do not substitute a convenient tag for the stated exact-content retrieval test.

video_need.reason: Publishing a tagged image and retrieving its exact digest under different identities benefits from an end-to-end terminal demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Using an already-built image, a sandbox ECR repository, supplied Region and registry values, and separately prepared approved publisher and consumer identities, authenticate Docker, tag and push the image, then retrieve its exact published digest as the consumer.
practice_anchor.success: The approved publisher authenticates using aws ecr get-login-password --region REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin REGISTRY and successfully pushes REGISTRY/REPOSITORY:TAG. The published digest is recorded. In the separately prepared consumer context, Docker authenticates and successfully retrieves REGISTRY/REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST with docker pull. The retrieved digest matches the published digest, and both identity-specific access outcomes are preserved.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the publisher's tagged push reference beside the consumer's digest-qualified pull reference, with the approved identity and successful access outcome for each. Make the matching published and retrieved digest visible.

teaching_notes: Require external Docker and shell-pipe preparation; commands are supplied-value templates.

context.concept_name: Publish a traceable immutable build artifact

coverage.learning_objective: Publish a traceable immutable build artifact

required_facts.statement: An artifact attestation binds provenance such as source repository, revision and build workflow to an artifact digest.

For a supplied output file, set workflow permissions id-token: write, contents: read and attestations: write, generate provenance with actions/attest@v4 and subject-path set to the file, then publish it with actions/upload-artifact@v4 using path set to that file and name set to the supplied revision-based version; retain the workflow run, artifact name and upload’s SHA256 digest as the immutable content reference, since v4 artifacts are immutable.

Download the published artifact with actions/download-artifact, which checks the upload’s SHA256 digest and warns on mismatch, then verify the extracted output file’s provenance with gh attestation verify PATH/TO/YOUR/BUILD/ARTIFACT-BINARY -R ORGANIZATION_NAME/REPOSITORY_NAME --format json and inspect the verified attestation for the source revision and build workflow/run before deployment.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A release needs more than a downloadable build file: the operator must connect the exact content with its source and build provenance. Follow one supplied output through attestation, immutable publication, download and provenance verification.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An artifact attestation binds provenance such as source repository, revision and build workflow to an artifact digest.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
For a supplied output file, set workflow permissions id-token: write, contents: read and attestations: write, generate provenance with actions/attest@v4 and subject-path set to the file, then publish it with actions/upload-artifact@v4 using path set to that file and name set to the supplied revision-based version; retain the workflow run, artifact name and upload’s SHA256 digest as the immutable content reference, since v4 artifacts are immutable.

Download the published artifact with actions/download-artifact, which checks the upload’s SHA256 digest and warns on mismatch, then verify the extracted output file’s provenance with gh attestation verify PATH/TO/YOUR/BUILD/ARTIFACT-BINARY -R ORGANIZATION_NAME/REPOSITORY_NAME --format json and inspect the verified attestation for the source revision and build workflow/run before deployment.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the supplied output is an orders release file for revision rev-42. Use that file as subject-path for actions/attest@v4 with the stated workflow permissions. Publish the same file through actions/upload-artifact@v4 using its path and the supplied revision-based name. Retain the workflow run, artifact name and upload SHA256 digest as the content reference. Download it through actions/download-artifact and inspect any digest-mismatch warning; that action checks the upload digest. Then run the stated gh attestation verify template on the extracted output file for the approved repository. Inspect the verified JSON attestation for source revision and build workflow/run before deployment. The example keeps download-integrity evidence and provenance evidence connected to the same output rather than treating either one alone as the entire traceability record.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A digest check and provenance verification answer different questions. Download checks the upload SHA256 digest and warns on mismatch; the verified attestation provides source and build context. Do not claim the download action itself blocks every mismatch or proves the intended source revision.

video_need.reason: Artifact upload, digest check and verified attestation provenance are linked evidence views that benefit from a single continuous demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Complete and execute a supplied GitHub Actions workflow to attest and publish the supplied orders release file for revision rev-42 under its supplied revision-based artifact name.
practice_anchor.success: The workflow attests and uploads the same supplied file with the required permissions and actions. The publication record retains the workflow run, revision-based artifact name and upload SHA256 digest as the immutable content reference.

live_code.required_skill: Configure provenance generation and immutable artifact publication in an established GitHub Actions workflow.
allowed_syntax: GitHub Actions YAML workflow, job and step structure
permissions: with id-token: write, contents: read and attestations: write
with: subject-path set to the supplied output file
with: path set to the supplied output file and name set to the supplied revision-based version
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an established runnable workflow, the already-built orders release file for rev-42, its exact path and supplied revision-based artifact name. Leave only the required permissions, attestation step and upload step incomplete.
live_code.observable_success: A completed workflow run generates provenance for the supplied file and publishes that same file through actions/upload-artifact@v4. The learner retains the run reference, supplied artifact name and upload SHA256 digest together.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the evidence linkage visible: the workflow run, revision-based artifact name and upload SHA256 digest; the download digest-check result; and the verified attestation for the extracted orders release file showing its artifact digest, source repository, revision rev-42 and build workflow/run.

teaching_notes: Use actions/attest@v4, not a substituted action; preserve the warning behavior and verify the extracted output file.

context.concept_name: Read and modify a standard CloudFormation S3 template; directly require the native S3 object-storage concept

required_facts.statement: A CloudFormation template’s Resources section declares resources by logical ID, Type and Properties.
An S3 bucket declaration uses Type: AWS::S3::Bucket; Ref on its logical ID returns its bucket name.
Modify the supplied declared property and references, validate with aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://TEMPLATE, and create the sandbox stack from the approved template.
Inspect stack events and outputs and the bucket’s live property to confirm the declaration was deployed.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied CloudFormation S3 template needs one approved property change. Read the declaration and references first, then verify that the live resource reflects the approved template rather than stopping at template validation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A CloudFormation template’s Resources section declares resources by logical ID, Type and Properties.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
An S3 bucket declaration uses Type: AWS::S3::Bucket; Ref on its logical ID returns its bucket name.

Modify the supplied declared property and references, validate with aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://TEMPLATE, and create the sandbox stack from the approved template.

Inspect stack events and outputs and the bucket’s live property to confirm the declaration was deployed.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Find the bucket's logical ID in Resources and inspect its Type and Properties. Type: AWS::S3::Bucket declares the bucket, and Ref on that logical ID returns its bucket name. Modify only the supplied property and references, then substitute the template file path in validate-template. Create the approved sandbox stack and inspect stack events and outputs. Finally, check the bucket's live value for the changed property. Keep declaration, deployment evidence and live-property evidence together: a correct-looking template is the requested state, while the live inspection checks what was deployed. This exercise uses the supplied standard template rather than introducing a new infrastructure language or unrelated resources.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Template validation is not verification of the bucket's live property. Inspect stack events, outputs and the deployed property after creating the sandbox stack. Also, Ref on an S3 bucket logical ID returns the bucket name, not an invented object reference.

video_need.reason: Template declaration, Ref output and live bucket-property verification benefit from an annotated template-to-stack demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Modify only the approved property and its supplied references in one standard CloudFormation S3 template. Validate the template, create its approved sandbox stack, and verify the bucket declaration against stack events, outputs and the live bucket property.
practice_anchor.success: The template declares one AWS::S3::Bucket resource, references resolve to the intended bucket logical ID, validation succeeds, and stack evidence and the live property confirm the approved change. Ref returns the deployed bucket name.

live_code.required_skill: Read and modify a supplied S3 resource declaration and Ref references, then validate and verify its sandbox deployment.
allowed_syntax: Properties and the supplied property key and approved value
Ref using the supplied bucket logical ID
Supplied stack-event, stack-output and S3 live-property inspection commands
blocked_syntax: New property keys beyond the supplied property
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide one standard template containing the supplied bucket logical ID, S3 resource type, property and Ref output. Include the approved property value, sandbox target and ready-to-use deployment and inspection commands.
live_code.observable_success: The edited template validates successfully; the sandbox stack provisions one bucket; its Ref output identifies that bucket; stack events and the bucket's live property confirm the approved declaration.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the connection visible between the supplied bucket's logical ID, Type and Properties, its Ref output, stack deployment evidence and the corresponding live bucket property.

context.concept_name: Select one evidence-backed delivery workflow improvement

coverage.learning_objective: Select an evidence-backed delivery workflow improvement

required_facts.statement: Continuous improvement uses feedback and measured outcomes to identify and address delivery friction.
Identify a bottleneck supported by the supplied delivery evidence and propose one bounded change with a measurable expected outcome.
Compare the success signal before and after the change to determine whether the intervention improved the intended outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A team has several complaints about delivery, but the exercise asks for one evidence-backed improvement. Select a bottleneck supported by the supplied record and define a measurable result before proposing the change.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Continuous improvement uses feedback and measured outcomes to identify and address delivery friction.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify a bottleneck supported by the supplied delivery evidence and propose one bounded change with a measurable expected outcome.

Compare the success signal before and after the change to determine whether the intervention improved the intended outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose supplied delivery records show that a particular review handoff is the measured bottleneck. Propose one bounded change to that handoff and state the success signal the evidence will compare. Record the baseline for that signal, apply the approved change, then compare the after-change signal with the baseline. If the chosen measure does not improve, do not call the intervention successful merely because the change was completed. Keep the conclusion about this bottleneck and measured outcome, not about every aspect of delivery. The example does not assume a particular improvement always works; feedback and measured results determine whether it helped.

If the after-change success signal worsens or remains unchanged, report that observed result instead of replacing the chosen measure with a more flattering one. The intervention was justified by one observed bottleneck and one expected outcome; the comparison should retain that same outcome. A completed action can be useful feedback even when it fails to produce the anticipated improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Implementing a change is not proof of improvement. Identify the evidence-supported bottleneck, state the expected measurable outcome and compare its success signal before and after. A general preference for automation is not the missing measurement.

video_need.reason: One bottleneck and its before/after success signal can be compared in a small evidence table without a tool demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Using supplied delivery records for a review handoff, select one evidence-supported bottleneck, one bounded handoff change, and a measurable success signal. Record the supplied baseline and compare it with the supplied after-change result.
practice_anchor.success: The selected bottleneck is supported by the records, the change addresses only that bottleneck, and the success signal measures the intended outcome without an invented target. The comparison uses the same signal before and after and reports whether it improved, remained unchanged, or worsened.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the review-handoff evidence, selected bottleneck, bounded change, and success signal visible together, including baseline and after-change values for the same measure.

teaching_notes: Use supplied delivery evidence; avoid inventing performance targets or attributing results to individuals.

required_facts.statement: AWS Config rules evaluate recorded resource configuration against desired conditions and report compliance results.
Open the rule’s noncompliant resources and inspect the affected resource, evaluation result and rule parameters to identify the configuration mismatch.
Choose the established remediation or escalation path from the governing policy rather than treating a compliance result as proof of an attack.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A Config rule reports a noncompliant resource. Before choosing a response, establish which recorded configuration differs from the rule's desired conditions and what the governing policy permits.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: AWS Config rules evaluate recorded resource configuration against desired conditions and report compliance results.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Open the rule’s noncompliant resources and inspect the affected resource, evaluation result and rule parameters to identify the configuration mismatch.

Choose the established remediation or escalation path from the governing policy rather than treating a compliance result as proof of an attack.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Open the supplied rule's noncompliant-resource result and record the resource identity. Compare the evaluation result and rule parameters with the affected resource's recorded configuration. Suppose the mismatch is a supplied setting outside the rule's required value; describe that setting mismatch rather than labeling the resource attacked. Choose the established remediation or escalation path from the governing policy. Preserve the evaluation evidence with that choice so the next operator can see why the response was selected. This is basic configuration-finding triage, not proof of malicious activity or permission to apply an unapproved change.

For a supplied noncompliant result, distinguish the rule's required value from the resource's recorded value. If the rule parameters differ from what the operator expected, include that discrepancy in triage rather than silently comparing with a different criterion. The governing policy determines whether the next action is remediation or escalation. The compliance evidence establishes a configuration mismatch, not an attacker or a cause of compromise.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A compliance result reports configuration against desired conditions; it is not proof of an attack. Read the resource, evaluation and parameters before choosing the policy-governed remediation or escalation path.

video_need.reason: A brief rule-result and recorded-configuration comparison helps locate mismatch evidence; the response decision remains explicit in text.

practice_anchor.objective: Triage one supplied AWS Config finding under an established policy by opening the rule's noncompliant resources, inspecting the affected resource's recorded configuration, evaluation result and rule parameters, and selecting the permitted remediation or escalation path.
practice_anchor.success: Identify the violated rule and affected resource, distinguish the rule's required value from the recorded value, and select the next action authorized by the supplied policy. Preserve the evaluation evidence supporting that choice without inferring an attack or applying an unapproved change.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied rule's noncompliant-resource result, resource identity, evaluation result, rule parameters and recorded configuration visible together so the required and recorded values can be compared and the mismatch located.

teaching_notes: Do not infer compromise or design specialist security remediation.

required_facts.statement: CloudFormation drift detection compares supported explicitly declared resource properties with their current values.
Run drift detection on the provisioned stack after the supplied out-of-band change, wait for completion and inspect the bucket’s expected and actual property values.
Drift detection reports differences without repairing them; unsupported or undeclared properties may not be checked.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A stack's bucket property was changed outside CloudFormation in the controlled lab. Drift detection can show a declared-versus-current difference, but the operator must understand what it checked and what it did not do.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudFormation drift detection compares supported explicitly declared resource properties with their current values.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run drift detection on the provisioned stack after the supplied out-of-band change, wait for completion and inspect the bucket’s expected and actual property values.

Drift detection reports differences without repairing them; unsupported or undeclared properties may not be checked.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Run drift detection on the provisioned stack after the supplied out-of-band change and wait for completion. Locate the bucket's result and compare its expected and actual property values. Write the difference as a pair, such as supplied declared value A and current value B, rather than saying only drifted. Detection compares supported explicitly declared properties; unsupported or undeclared properties may not be checked. Keep that scope beside the result so a lack of reported drift is not described as exhaustive verification of every property. This task observes and records the difference. It does not repair the resource merely by running detection.

A useful drift record names the stack resource, the specific checked property and its expected/actual pair. If another setting is not explicitly declared or supported for comparison, do not infer its correctness from this result. This lets the next operator see exactly what detection established. Running detection again without changing the resource does not perform the missing repair; detection and approved correction are different actions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Drift detection reports differences without repairing them. It also does not promise to check every property: supported, explicitly declared properties are the comparison scope, and unsupported or undeclared properties may not be checked.

video_need.reason: Expected-versus-actual resource properties and drift-detection status benefit from a before-and-after inspection demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Provision one S3 bucket in a sandbox using the supplied CloudFormation template. Apply the supplied out-of-band change to one supported, explicitly declared bucket property, run stack drift detection, wait for completion, and inspect the bucket's expected and actual property values.
practice_anchor.success: Provide evidence of the provisioned bucket and completed drift detection, identifying the stack resource, checked property, and expected/actual value pair. Explain that detection reports the difference without repairing it and does not establish the correctness of unsupported or undeclared properties.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the bucket's explicitly declared property value and its changed live value visible side by side, together with the completed detection status and resource drift result.

teaching_notes: Keep detection distinct from repair; do not extend drift coverage beyond supported declared properties.

coverage.learning_objective: Recover a failed CloudFormation EC2 stack update

required_facts.statement: CloudFormation stack events record resource operation status and failure reasons during an update.
After the supplied controlled update failure, inspect the first failing resource event and subsequent rollback events.
UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE indicates rollback to the previous working stack state; UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED requires resolving the rollback failure before continuing.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A controlled stack update failed. The response needs both the original failure evidence and the rollback outcome; a final stack label alone can hide the sequence that explains the problem.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudFormation stack events record resource operation status and failure reasons during an update.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
After the supplied controlled update failure, inspect the first failing resource event and subsequent rollback events.

UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE indicates rollback to the previous working stack state; UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED requires resolving the rollback failure before continuing.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the supplied update's stack events, starting with the first failing resource event and its failure reason. Then follow subsequent rollback events. If the resulting status is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, describe rollback to the previous working stack state. If it is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, the rollback failure must be resolved before continuing. Retain the first failure and the rollback status separately in the record so that the update problem is not confused with a later rollback problem. Use the supplied controlled failure and approved response path rather than experimenting with new changes while the rollback outcome is unresolved.

For an illustrative event sequence, suppose the update first reports a resource failure and later reports a rollback failure. The first event explains why the requested update did not complete; the later event explains why rollback did not complete. Preserve both reasons in their event order. Resolving only the first update problem does not justify ignoring the status that says rollback failure still needs resolution before continuing.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED is not another success label for rollback. It requires resolving the rollback failure before continuing. Conversely, UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE describes rollback to the prior working stack state, not successful deployment of the failed update.

video_need.reason: The first failure and subsequent rollback events form a changing sequence best clarified through one controlled stack update.

practice_anchor.objective: Use a supplied CloudFormation stack template to provision one EC2 instance in a prepared sandbox simulation. Apply the supplied controlled update-failure scaffolding, inspect the first failing resource event and its failure reason, and follow subsequent rollback events to determine the final stack state.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied stack initially provisions one EC2 instance. After the controlled update failure, the learner records the first failing resource event and its reason separately from subsequent rollback events, and verifies that UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE indicates return to the previous working stack state. For a supplied UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED event sequence, the learner identifies that the rollback failure requires resolution through established guidance before continuing.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the CloudFormation stack events and final stack status visible together, with event order, resource operation statuses, and failure reasons distinguishable so the original update failure can be traced through subsequent rollback events.

teaching_notes: Do not invent failure-recovery commands; inspect supplied events and established resolution guidance.

required_facts.statement: An instance profile contains one IAM role and provides a way to pass that role to EC2.
Attach or replace the approved instance profile on the EC2 instance using the instance’s IAM-role setting or associate-iam-instance-profile.
Use the instance’s role credential provider rather than embedded keys, inspect the caller identity and test one allowed and one denied operation under the assigned role’s permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An EC2 application needs the approved role rather than embedded access keys. Attach the role through its instance profile, then test the resulting identity and bounded permissions from the instance.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An instance profile contains one IAM role and provides a way to pass that role to EC2.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use associate-iam-instance-profile to attach the approved instance profile to an EC2 instance without an existing association. To replace an existing profile, use the console’s Modify IAM role workflow instead.

Use the instance’s role credential provider rather than embedded keys, inspect the caller identity and test one allowed and one denied operation under the assigned role’s permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For attachment to an instance without an existing association, use the supplied associate-iam-instance-profile operation. For replacement of an existing profile, use the console’s Modify IAM role workflow to select the approved role. The profile contains one IAM role. From the instance, use the role credential provider, inspect caller identity and test one supplied allowed operation and one denied operation. Record the assigned role context with those outcomes. Merely seeing an attached profile is not the full permission test for the application.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An instance profile is the container used to pass one role to EC2, not a reason to embed keys. Test application operations under the role credential provider and inspect caller identity rather than assuming the attachment proves the intended access.

video_need.reason: A short profile-attachment and caller/permission check helps locate the relevant identity evidence, while text specifies both tests.

required_facts.statement: EKS Pod Identity associates a Kubernetes service account in a namespace and cluster with an IAM role for application AWS access.

teaching_blocks.content: EKS Pod Identity associates a Kubernetes service account in a namespace and cluster with an IAM role for application AWS access.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create an association for the supplied cluster, namespace, service account and approved role; run the workload with that serviceAccountName.

The Pod Identity agent and supported SDK credential chain supply temporary role credentials to associated Pods; verify allowed access from the intended workload and rejection from an unassociated workload.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Create the approved Pod Identity association using the supplied cluster, namespace, service account and role. Run the workload with that serviceAccountName. The Pod Identity agent and supported SDK credential chain supply temporary role credentials to associated Pods. teaching_blocks.content: A role's existence is not the workload association. The association names a service account in a namespace and cluster, and the workload must use that serviceAccountName. Preserve the agent and supported-SDK qualifications when describing credential delivery.

practice_anchor.success: The association matches the supplied cluster, namespace, service account and approved role; the intended workload uses that serviceAccountName. With the supplied Pod Identity agent and supported SDK credential chain, the intended workload's approved AWS operation succeeds and the unassociated workload's attempt is rejected. context.concept_name: Configure GitHub Actions AWS role federation

coverage.learning_objective: Configure GitHub Actions OIDC federation to an AWS role

required_facts.statement: GitHub Actions OIDC enables a workflow to obtain temporary AWS role credentials without storing AWS access keys.
Configure the GitHub token issuer as an IAM OIDC provider and constrain the role trust policy’s aud and sub claims to the approved audience and repository/branch or environment.
Give the workflow id-token: write permission and configure the AWS credential action to assume the approved role; test that an unapproved repository or branch cannot assume it.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A GitHub Actions workflow should enter an approved AWS role without stored AWS access keys. The trust boundary must identify the approved token context rather than accepting any workflow that can request a token.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: GitHub Actions OIDC enables a workflow to obtain temporary AWS role credentials without storing AWS access keys.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the GitHub token issuer as an IAM OIDC provider and constrain the role trust policy’s aud and sub claims to the approved audience and repository/branch or environment.

Give the workflow id-token: write permission and configure the AWS credential action to assume the approved role; test that an unapproved repository or branch cannot assume it.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the supplied GitHub token issuer as the IAM OIDC provider. In the role trust policy, compare aud and sub with the approved audience and repository/branch or environment. Give the workflow id-token: write permission and configure the supplied AWS credential action to assume that role. Then run the approved case and the supplied unapproved repository or branch case. Verify the latter cannot assume the role. This test makes the trust scope observable rather than treating temporary credentials alone as evidence that only the intended workflow can get them.

The negative test should differ in the repository, branch or environment context that the supplied sub condition restricts. A successful approved case plus a rejected unapproved case supports that exact trust boundary. Check the audience separately rather than treating a matching subject as evidence that every trust test passed. The AWS credential action's success must be read with the approved token context and role target.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Avoiding stored keys does not remove the trust-policy check. Constrain aud and sub to the approved context and test an unapproved repository or branch. A workflow's id-token permission alone does not establish the intended AWS role trust boundary.

video_need.reason: Audience/subject trust restrictions and approved/unapproved workflow tests benefit from annotated policy and workflow context.

practice_anchor.success: The approved workflow obtains temporary credentials for the intended role without stored AWS keys. The supplied unapproved repository or branch case cannot assume that role, and the configured audience condition separately matches only the approved audience.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the IAM OIDC provider, trust-policy aud and sub conditions, workflow id-token: write permission, and AWS credentials action role target visible together with the approved and unapproved test contexts.

teaching_notes: Keep this GitHub OIDC mechanism separate from CodePipeline service-role trust.

coverage.learning_objective: Obtain and inspect an STS session

required_facts.statement: Temporary AWS credentials consist of an access key ID, secret access key and session token and expire after their issued lifetime.
Call aws sts assume-role with --role-arn, --role-session-name and the approved --duration-seconds, then use all three returned credential fields and inspect Expiration.

Permissions granted through a role’s identity-based policies are intersected with any session policies; resource-based grants are evaluated separately, and grants directly to the session ARN are not limited by session policies; an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides an allow.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operator assumes an approved role for a bounded session. The returned credentials have three fields and an expiry, and the permissions explanation must keep role-policy grants distinct from resource-based grants.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Temporary AWS credentials consist of an access key ID, secret access key and session token and expire after their issued lifetime.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Call aws sts assume-role with --role-arn, --role-session-name and the approved --duration-seconds, then use all three returned credential fields and inspect Expiration.

Permissions granted through a role’s identity-based policies are intersected with any session policies; resource-based grants are evaluated separately, and grants directly to the session ARN are not limited by session policies; an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides an allow.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Substitute the approved role ARN, session name and duration in the assume-role command. Use the returned access key ID, secret access key and session token together, and inspect Expiration. If a session policy is supplied, role identity-policy permissions are intersected with it. Do not extend that sentence to every resource grant: resource-based grants are evaluated separately, and grants directly to the session ARN are not limited by session policies. An applicable explicit deny still overrides an allow. Record the issued lifetime and the supplied permission evidence without displaying credential values. This example teaches session composition and the stated grant distinctions, not a new policy intended to exercise every possible permission case.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Temporary credentials are not just an access-key pair: the session token is also required, and the issued lifetime ends. Likewise, session-policy intersection describes role identity-based grants; it is not an unqualified limit on all resource-based grants.

video_need.reason: Session lifetime and identity/session/resource-grant distinctions benefit from a credential timeline and policy-evaluation diagram.

practice_anchor.objective: Assume one trusted sandbox role using aws sts assume-role with the supplied approved --role-arn, --role-session-name and --duration-seconds. Inspect the returned credential field names and Expiration, then configure the session using all three credential fields without displaying their values.
practice_anchor.success: The request matches the approved role, session name and duration. All three returned credential fields are used, their values remain concealed, and the recorded Expiration and issued lifetime match the approved duration. Using supplied permission evidence, distinguish role identity-policy grants intersected with any session policy from separately evaluated resource-based grants, preserve the direct-session-ARN exception, and apply any applicable explicit deny.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a bounded credential timeline with access key ID, secret access key and session token represented by field names only, ending at Expiration. Alongside it, distinguish role identity-policy grants intersected with session policies from separately evaluated resource-based grants; explicitly show that direct session-ARN grants are not limited by session policies and that an applicable explicit deny overrides an allow.

teaching_notes: Do not expose credential values; preserve direct-session-ARN and explicit-deny qualifications.

context.concept_name: Authorize an event target with least-privilege execution permissions

coverage.learning_objective: Authorize an event target execution role

required_facts.statement: EventBridge target execution authority is separate from the event pattern that selects events.
For targets requiring an execution role, grant events.amazonaws.com permission to assume the role and attach permissions scoped to the approved target operation and resource.
Targets such as SNS and Lambda use resource-based permissions for invocation; use the target’s required authorization model rather than assuming every target uses a role.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An event pattern matches the right event, but that does not authorize the target operation. Determine the target's required permission model before assigning execution authority.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: EventBridge target execution authority is separate from the event pattern that selects events.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
For targets requiring an execution role, grant events.amazonaws.com permission to assume the role and attach permissions scoped to the approved target operation and resource.

Targets such as SNS and Lambda use resource-based permissions for invocation; use the target’s required authorization model rather than assuming every target uses a role.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
For a supplied target that requires an execution role, grant events.amazonaws.com the approved trust to assume it and scope role permissions to the approved operation and resource. For a supplied SNS or Lambda target, use the required resource-based invocation permissions instead. Compare the selected target with its authorization model in the record. The selection pattern determines which events match; the separate authority determines whether the intended target operation is permitted. Do not assign a role to every target just because a different target used one.

For a target requiring an execution role, inspect both trust and scoped operation/resource permission. Trust permits EventBridge to assume the role; the role's permissions cover the approved target action. For the SNS or Lambda case, inspect the resource-based invocation permission instead. These are different authorization records even if the same event pattern selects the event, which is why matching alone cannot verify target execution authority.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Event selection and execution permission are separate. SNS and Lambda use resource-based invocation permissions in this brief, so assuming every target uses an execution role misstates the authorization model.

video_need.reason: The choice between execution-role and resource-based target permission models benefits from a rule-to-target authorization diagram.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure authorization for a supplied EventBridge target using its stated permission model, approved action, and resource. For a role-based target, configure EventBridge trust and scoped role permissions; for an SNS or Lambda target, configure the supplied resource-based invocation permission.
practice_anchor.success: The authorization record uses the target's required model and permits only the supplied bounded action on the supplied resource. A role-based target includes trust for events.amazonaws.com and scoped operation permissions; an SNS or Lambda target uses resource-based invocation permission. The event pattern remains unchanged.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show event-pattern matching separately from target authorization, with one authorization branch for events.amazonaws.com assuming an execution role with scoped action/resource permissions and another for SNS or Lambda resource-based invocation permissions.

teaching_notes: Use supplied targets and least-privilege permissions; do not invent target operations.

clusters.title: Publishing exact release content
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts are two forms of publishing and retrieving exact release content: a container image in ECR and a provenance-linked build file. All recorded prerequisites precede the tile; required external Docker, shell and workflow preparation must also be complete before entry. Keep the ECR digest and authentication procedure separate from GitHub artifact immutability and attestation verification: shared presentation compares publication workflows, not interchangeable tools or guarantees.
